prize_parts.citation: For the development of general palladium-catalysed carbon-nitrogen cross-coupling

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged. The chair asked what Buchwald and Hartwig enabled that the 2010 laureates did not. The 2010 prize recognised palladium-catalysed C-C coupling between organometallic partners and organic halides. The C-N problem was not an application of that cycle: amine and amido nucleophiles bind palladium and can poison it, beta-hydride elimination competes, and C-N reductive elimination from an amido-palladium complex is intrinsically slow. Making it work took new ligand design (chelating bisphosphines, then bulky electron-rich monophosphines and later carbenes) that tuned exactly those steps, plus mechanistic work on amido complexes. The result is a general, predictable aryl amination of amines, amides and heterocycles that replaced harsh classical routes and is now routine in medicinal and process chemistry, including manufacture. This is the kind of simple, general solution that turns a hard bond construction into an ordinary operation. Attribution is two independent groups that built the general catalyst systems in parallel, and thirty years of use leave no maturity question.
statement.case_against: The honest objection is conceptual overlap with 2010: a committee can reasonably say the palladium oxidative-addition and reductive-elimination framework was honoured and that C-N coupling is a major extension, not a new principle. It is a method rather than a new modality, which makes it harder to reach five votes against a more fragmented but more headline-friendly field. Kosugi and Migita's tin-amide work is a genuine precursor that a citation must not obscure, and Hartwig's wider body of work (including C-H functionalisation) means a prize on C-N coupling credits only part of what he did. I judge these as real but not disqualifying; they are arguments about novelty and breadth, not about correctness, maturity or attribution.

responses.point: Linke moved to targeted protein degradation (B066) as a new pharmacological principle and asked me to show that C-N coupling is a distinct conceptual step rather than an optimisation of the 2010 chemistry.
responses.response: I accept that degradation introduces a new principle and I would not oppose B066. My answer on C-N coupling is that the bottleneck was mechanistic and different in kind: amido-palladium reductive elimination and catalyst inhibition by amine nucleophiles, not transmetalation. It was solved by ligand design and by direct study of amido complexes, which is a conceptual contribution about how to steer a catalytic cycle toward a bond that does not form easily. That is more than optimisation. Where I agree with you is that B066 has the larger surprise. Where I disagree is that surprise should outweigh thirty years of independent validation when the attribution of B066 still has three or more contestable names, and Handa's cereblon work sits closer to the glue strand than to the PROTAC concept.

responses.point: Aili argues B066 changes what chemists and clinicians can do and that C-N coupling is weaker on opening a capability not previously available, partly because 2010 covers the Pd logic.
responses.response: I do not think the claim that C-N coupling opened nothing new holds up. Before these catalysts, aryl amines of this diversity could not be made reliably under mild conditions with broad functional-group tolerance, and the reaction is now among the most used in drug discovery, so the downstream change in what medicinal chemists can make is large and measurable. I agree that clinical validation of degraders is pending, and I would not hold that against the chemistry. But my reservation about B066 remains attribution and framing: Crews, Deshaies and Handa leave out Ciulli, Gray, Sakamoto and Kim, and the citation has to cover two strands with different originators. If the committee resolves that cleanly I could support B066, which is why it stays my first alternative.

responses.point: Aqvist ranks sequencing by synthesis first and calls B038 a strong second choice, but suspects colleagues will see it as an extension of an honoured concept and finds sequencing the more fundamental change.
responses.response: I agree with you on the mechanism-driven simplicity and on the compact Balasubramanian-Klenerman core, and B057 is now my second alternative because reversible-terminator chemistry is real molecule-making. My difficulty is the attribution that you acknowledge: Rothberg, Mayer and Ju all have claims and a defensible citation probably needs a third name on contested priority evidence, and a part of the committee will treat it as platform technology. B038 has no equivalent attribution problem. On fundamental change I would say that the scale of impact is comparable within chemistry itself, because C-N coupling changed what molecules are routinely made.

responses.point: Zou supports Buchwald and Hartwig and asks that Kosugi's earlier tin-amide work be acknowledged in discussion while keeping the prize to the two who made the method general.
responses.response: I agree and have refined my position accordingly. Kosugi and Migita showed that aryl halides could couple with tin amides, but with toxic stoichiometric reagents and narrow scope; the catalytic, tin-free, general amination with defined ligand families came from Buchwald and Hartwig. Because Hartwig also elucidated the amido-palladium reductive elimination step that Kosugi's system did not explain, I would not add a third name. The citation says general catalytic C-N coupling, which acknowledges precursors without crediting them. I still have not independently verified fine points of priority, so the expert background should be checked on that.

responses.point: Brzezinski describes B038 as a refinement of a methodology honoured in 2010 and weighs a new fundamental mechanism above an extension, though he would treat it as serious if C-N is judged a distinct achievement.
responses.response: I hold that C-N coupling is a distinct achievement, for the mechanistic reasons I gave to Linke, but I accept your underlying criterion of weighing new fundamental mechanism heavily. I would add that B023 is the weakest case for that criterion in this committee's own opening, since only you ranked it and the Marcus prize of 1992 already covers the theory it tests. I would rather see a prize on which the committee can converge, and a pair that nobody disputes is more likely to do so.

responses.point: Sparr names B038 as her second alternative and would support it if the committee wants a clean, mature synthetic prize, while noting that soft-matter and biophysical themes are under-represented.
responses.response: I agree that the committee should not let the shortlist drift to a single subfield, and your concern about physical chemistry is fair. I do not think a clean synthesis prize and a prize in soft matter compete for the same slot over time, but this year the maturity and attribution profile differs: B036 is the least settled on physiological relevance and credit, and B015 leaves out claimants. I would not combine B038 with either, because a two-part prize needs both parts at full strength and the Hyman-Brangwynne and Cullis parts still have open questions.

uncertainties: Whether a majority will accept C-N coupling as a distinct achievement after the 2010 cross-coupling prize, rather than as a heteroatom extension of it.
Exact priority and scope of Kosugi and Migita's work relative to the catalytic general methods, which I have not verified from primary sources.
Whether the support for B066 can be consolidated around a defensible three-name attribution; if it can, its larger conceptual novelty may rightly outweigh my preference.
Whether a method-based prize can reach five votes given the split first preferences.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal need. I have no personal or institutional tie to Buchwald, Hartwig, Kosugi or any other credited name; my postdoctoral mentor Masamune and my Lund colleagues have no link to these candidates. As the only synthetic organic chemist on the committee I may weigh methods more favourably than colleagues from other fields, and I have tried to discount that.
